Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

You know that feeling when it’s two in the afternoon, and you can’t quite account for where the morning went? Not because you weren’t doing things, but because the busyness didn’t add up to anything you can point to.

It’s demoralizing in a specific way, and it has surprisingly little to do with how early your alarm went off. Time management experts Melinda Rathkopf, M.D., M.B.A., and Julie Morgenstern, the author of multiple bestselling books on productivity, say most of what shapes your morning was set in motion the night before, and the solution is usually far simpler than the elaborate routines you’ve seen floating around online.

Where do both experts begin? The evening before. When you make decisions about tomorrow before you go to sleep, you take some of the friction out of the morning itself. “Preplanning the day ahead and making decisions ahead of time makes the rest of your day potentially calmer and less stressful,” says Rathkopf. “Set yourself up by knowing what’s coming.”

Transition time is one of the things that tends to get left out when people plan their days. It’s easy to schedule back-to-back tasks and forget that moving between them really does take time. Build that in the night before and the morning feels a lot less like you’re already behind before you’ve started.

This extends to sleep, too. Rathkopf recommends starting with how much sleep you genuinely need to feel refreshed, then working backward from your wake time to set a consistent bedtime. “Sleep is so vital to daily functioning and brain health,” she says. Most people schedule everything else first and try to fit sleep in around it. She suggests reversing that.

If there’s one habit both experts come back to, it’s keeping your phone out of your first and last hour of each day. Morgenstern is direct about it. “The number one thing that can boost morning productivity has to do with screen time,” she says. “We should not be on our devices an hour before bed, and we should not be on our devices for our first hour of the morning.”

Checking your phone first thing does more than eat up time. It pulls you into a reactive state before you’ve had a chance to figure out your own priorities for the day. “The phone can be a useful tool, but it’s designed to keep us on there,” Morgenstern says. “Think of it like sugar — you have to really manage your consumption, and take charge.
